<reason>Side A won by establishing a concrete causal chain—jail stints destroy physical tolerance leading to fatal post-release overdoses, while criminal records lock users out of legal employment and manufacture the economic desperation that drives property crime. Side A successfully exposed that Side B's defense of "punitive enforcement" ultimately relied on non-criminal medical interventions (civil commitment, clinical mandates) that remain fully available under decriminalization, effectively collapsing Side B's distinction between the two policies. Side B's incentive-based arguments were strong but relied on abstract aggregate-effects reasoning that failed to neutralize Side A's specific physiological mechanism, and Side B contained a reference error ([C2.2, C2.4]) in Rebuttal 2.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Pressure Questions forced Side B to define the "coercive backstop" as graduated clinical intervention and medical detention rather than criminal jail time, allowing Side A to argue in the Closing that Side B had conceded the entire debate by stripping away the criminal element that defines "punitive enforcement" and replacing it with health tools available under decriminalization.</best_rebuttal>
